To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the famine was not caused by a lack of early warning, but rather by a failure of early action, that the failure to take early action was caused by a combination of factors, including a lack of political will, a lack of resources, a lack of capacity, a lack of coordination, and a lack of accountability, and that the famine was a failure of the international system of humanitarian assistance, not a failure of the Somali people.
the famine in Somalia in 2009-2011 was predictable, preventable and predictable.
early warning was not followed by early action because of the absence of an adequate and timely response by the international community to the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Somalia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the failure of the international system of famine prevention to live up to its own standards.
the question of whether the international system of early warning and emergency response is fit for purpose.
the question of why early warning information was not acted upon, and what can be learned from the Somalia experience to improve the timeliness of response to famine and food crises.

the international community failed to act on the early warning signs of famine.
early warning is a necessary but not sufficient component of famine prevention.
the international response to early warning in 2011 was late, and that this was a failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have to be much more realistic about the capacity of the international system to respond to early warnings, and that the international community needs to be much more honest about the fact that the international system is not capable of responding to all early warnings, and in particular, to early warning information that is not accompanied by an immediate, adequate and appropriate response from the national government.
we need to do more to support early warning systems, and that we need to support them better.
the international response was too late and not large enough.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 2011 famine was a failure of the international system of famine response, not of the early warning systems or the humanitarian response in Somalia itself.
, despite the many improvements in early warning systems over the past two decades, the international community is still failing to act on early warning information in a timely and effective manner.
